summary: Specifies an RTCP Extended Report block giving per-packet reports of packets discarded from the de-jitter buffer after successful reception. This gives senders extra insight into how a stream is being received.

eli5.summary: A receiver reports which pieces of a video call it threw away.

questions: what is the rtcp xr discard rle report block
how does rtcp report discarded packets
subtitle: An RTCP report block that tells a media sender exactly which received packets the receiver threw away.

tldr.problem: Existing RTCP reports can count discarded packets but cannot say which ones were discarded. Deriving that from frequent counts or gap/burst reports needs too much reporting or too much complexity.
tldr.mechanism: A new Extended Report block, Discard RLE (block type 25), reuses the run-length encoding of RFC 3611 to list discarded packets by sequence number. An E bit separates packets discarded for arriving too early from those discarded for arriving too late.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can precisely report discards from the de-jitter buffer, and senders can use the detail to adapt, but must work fine without any such reports.

today: RFC 7097 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reporting Discarded Packets
sections.content:
RTP carries real-time media such as audio and video, and RTCP gives feedback about what receivers see. RFC 3611 defines RTCP Extended Reports (XR) for more detail than the basic Receiver Report offers. One of its blocks, Loss Run Length Encoding (RLE), reports which packets were received and lost.

RFC 3611 also introduces discarded packets: packets that arrived but were dropped from the de-jitter buffer because they were too early for buffering or too late for playout. The discard rate in the VoIP metrics block counts them as a fraction, but not which ones.

Related extensions report the number of discarded packets (RFC 7002) or gaps and bursts of discards (RFC 7003). None identify specific packets. Getting there with high-frequency counts would take too much reporting and still be imprecise, and the gap/burst report adds complexity and overhead. This document applies the run-length idea from RFC 3611 to discarded packets.
sections.eli5: Counting how many cards you tossed does not tell the sender which ones. This lets you hand back the exact list.

sections.title: The Discard RLE Report Block
sections.content:
The block uses the same format as the loss and duplicate RLE blocks of RFC 3611. The fields BT, T, block length, SSRC of source, begin_seq and end_seq keep their RFC 3611 meaning. The chunks have the same run-length representation, but they describe discarded packets, as defined in RFC 7002.

The block type BT is the constant 25. The 3-bit rsvd field MUST be zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The new E bit says why packets were discarded: it is 1 if the chunks represent packets that arrived too early, and 0 otherwise (too late).

To report both early and late discards, a receiver MUST include two blocks. Their sequence number ranges MAY overlap, but each packet MUST be reported as only early or late. Packets that appear in both blocks are ignored, and packets in neither are considered properly received. Discard RLE blocks SHOULD be sent in a compound RTCP packet with a Receiver Report.
sections.eli5: The list is written in a compact way: it says things like a stretch of packets was kept, then a stretch was tossed. A little flag says whether the tossed ones were early or late.

sections.title: Receiver and Sender Behavior
sections.content:
Sending Discard RLE blocks is up to the media receiver, as is the reporting granularity. It is RECOMMENDED that the receiver report all discarded packets this way. If every packet in a reporting period was discarded, the receiver MAY use the Discard Report Block of RFC 7002 instead. When reporting bandwidth is limited, the receiver decides whether to include these blocks at all.

The blocks MAY go in regularly scheduled RTCP packets per RFC 3550, or in immediate or early feedback packets per RFC 4585.

The media sender MUST be prepared to operate without any Discard RLE blocks and cannot count on receiving all of them or on a regular pattern. If the sender gets XR reports without such blocks and knows the receiver supports them, it MAY assume no packets were discarded.
sections.eli5: The receiver decides when to send the list, and the sender must not depend on it. If the sender knows the receiver can send lists and none come, it may guess nothing was tossed.

sections.title: Signaling Support in SDP
sections.content: Participants MAY announce support in SDP or use the block without prior signaling. When SDP is used, the rtcp-xr attribute from RFC 3611 MUST be used, and its xr-format list gains a new parameter, discard-rle, which indicates support for the block. In an offer/answer exchange, the RFC 3611 rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters apply.
sections.eli5: Before the game starts, each side can say it knows how to send and read these lists, by writing a short keyword in its call description.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Per-packet statistics carry the confidentiality risk described in RFC 3611. Very detailed error information can also give an attacker insight into security processing. Where security matters, implementations should encrypt and authenticate the block, for example with the AVPF profile together with the Secure RTP profile as the combined SAVPF (RFC 5124, building on RFC 3711). The security considerations of RFC 3550, RFC 3611 and RFC 4585 also apply.
sections.eli5: A detailed list tells outsiders a lot about your call, so if that matters, the list should be locked in an envelope.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigns value 25 to DRLE (Discard RLE Report) in the RTCP XR Block Type registry. The document also registers discard-rle in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters. Appendix A restates the metric using the RFC 6390 template, including that measurement happens at the receiving end of the RTP stream.
sections.eli5: The new report gets its own official number and keyword so nobody else reuses them.

viz.caption: RTCP XR DISCARD RLE REPORT BLOCK (RFC 7097)

fields.name: rsvd
fields.desc: Reserved; MUST be zero and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: 1 if the chunks are packets discarded for arriving too early, 0 otherwise.

fields.name: begin_seq
fields.desc: Start of the reported sequence number range.

fields.name: end_seq
fields.desc: End of the reported sequence number range.

fields.name: chunk 2
fields.desc: Further chunks follow up to chunk n.
